title: Coral and the Horizon
premise: Jude Hartwell, caretaker of Earth's abandoned seed vault, has spent seven years hauling cargo through contested orbits to stay invisible—until the colony's children begin sharing a dream of a voice calling from the dead-space relay. The dream is a distress signal from the relay's last operator, Dr. Amara Voss, who is also the woman Jude loved and abandoned when she fled Earth's collapse. Racing a decaying signal that will soon be lost forever, Jude must choose between her duty to protect the vault's seeds—the last insurance for humanity—and the truth about why she left. At the relay, Jude finds Amara alive but fading, uploads the children's shared dream as a living memory archive, and chooses love over duty by broadcasting the vault's location, ending her invisibility but giving the colonies a future rooted in both memory and truth.
about_author: Yara Eastwick is a former marine cartographer who spent a decade mapping coastlines before turning to fiction about people adrift between worlds. She writes from a converted lighthouse keeper's cottage, where the horizon remains her favorite character.

chapters.title: The Weight of Quiet Cargo
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. A routine haul of seed crates through contested orbit establishes her careful invisibility: no names logged, no questions answered. When a dockhand mentions the colony children 'dreaming in unison,' Jude dismisses it—but her hands shake. Emotional beat: the cost of a life built on not being seen.

chapters.title: Children Who Dream the Same Sea
chapters.summary: Colony teacher Idris Okonkwo's POV. He records eleven children describing an identical dream: a woman's voice counting down inside a metal corridor full of water-light. The colony council wants it studied; Idris only wants to know why his daughter whispers a stranger's name—'Amara.' Emotional beat: wonder curdling into unease.

chapters.title: Seven Years of Not Looking Back
chapters.summary: Jude's POV, flashback woven into present. Maintaining the vault alone, she catalogues seeds labeled in handwriting she recognizes: Amara Voss's. The dream reports reach the vault via supply manifest gossip, and Jude realizes the voice belongs to the woman she left behind on dying Earth. Emotional beat: guilt resurfacing like a body in water.

chapters.title: The Council Wants Answers
chapters.summary: Councilor Bren Hale's POV. Hale sees the shared dream as either contagion or weapon and orders all cargo runners interrogated—including the reclusive vault caretaker. Jude learns she has forty-eight hours before officials arrive. Emotional beat: the walls of invisibility closing in.

chapters.title: What the Signal Remembers
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. Decoding fragments of the dream pattern, she isolates coordinates at the edge of dead space: Relay Station Kestrel, officially decommissioned nine years ago. The signal isn't a haunting—it's a countdown, and it's nearly finished. Emotional beat: terror and hope arriving together.

chapters.title: Manifests and Lies
chapters.summary: Idris's POV. He confronts Jude at the vault, having traced her false shipping records. She admits nothing, but he leaves his daughter's dream-drawing behind—a child's sketch of two women holding hands under a falling sky. Emotional beat: being known against one's will.

chapters.title: Stowaway
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. Fleeing ahead of the council's investigators, Jude discovers Idris's daughter Nia hiding among the seed crates—drawn by the dream, insisting 'the lady in the wall' needs them. Turning back means arrest; continuing means smuggling a child toward dead space. Emotional beat: reluctant responsibility.

chapters.title: Contested Orbit
chapters.summary: Nia's POV. From a crawl space, she watches pirates board Jude's hauler demanding tribute. Jude bargains with contraband memories—old Earth recordings—to pass. Nia realizes the fierce, closed-off pilot is afraid of something worse than pirates. Emotional beat: seeing an adult's fear clearly for the first time.

chapters.title: The Edge of Dead Space
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. Beyond the last beacon, navigation fails and they drift by dead reckoning. Jude finally tells Nia about Amara—not the official story, but the truth: she was ordered to evacuate alone and chose obedience over love. Emotional beat: confession as first act of courage.

chapters.title: Kestrel Breach
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. They dock with the derelict relay, its corridors flooded with failing coolant mist—the water-light from the dreams. Systems are half-alive, maintained by hand for years. Someone has been keeping it running. Emotional beat: dread sharpening into urgency.

chapters.title: The Woman in the Wall
chapters.summary: Amara's POV. Trapped since the evacuation cutoff, she turned the relay into a transmitter and seeded the dream signal through every colony network, betting someone would come. Her oxygen is nearly gone; her logs reveal she never blamed Jude. Emotional beat: endurance as an act of faith.

chapters.title: Reunion in the Mist
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. Jude finds Amara barely conscious in the transmitter core. Their reunion is angry, tender, and too brief—Amara reveals the real crisis: the relay holds Earth's final memory archive, and its power dies in three days. Emotional beat: love arriving too late to be simple.

chapters.title: What We Buried on Earth
chapters.summary: Amara's POV. She explains the archive contains not just data but recorded human memory—generations of it—and the council will seal or destroy it as a security risk if they find it first. The children's dreams were her message: remember us. Emotional beat: truth versus institutional loyalty.

chapters.title: Hale Arrives Early
chapters.summary: Bren Hale's POV. The council ship intercepts Kestrel; Hale boards with marines, declaring the station quarantined and the archive state property. He orders Jude detained for desertion and theft of vault resources. Emotional beat: duty weaponized.

chapters.title: The Choice in the Core
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. Locked in the vault bay while Hale's team strips the station, Jude must decide: stay silent and keep her clean record, or claim the archive openly. Nia's presence forces the question—who is she protecting, really? Emotional beat: the moment loyalty and truth split apart.

chapters.title: Signal Fire
chapters.summary: Amara's POV, weakening. With hours left, she begins manually broadcasting the memory archive wideband—open to everyone, uncontrollable by any council. Each transmission costs her remaining strength. Emotional beat: sacrifice without martyrdom, done matter-of-factly.

chapters.title: Mutiny of Small Hands
chapters.summary: Nia's POV. Nia slips her bonds and frees Jude using tricks learned from watching cargo runners. Together they reach the core just as Hale's engineers sever the antenna. The children across the colonies wake screaming as the dream cuts off. Emotional beat: a child's courage shaming adult caution.

chapters.title: Climax: The Broadcast
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. In the storm of the severed array, Jude physically reconnects the antenna while Hale orders her shot; Idris, aboard as Hale's translator, refuses the order and turns the marines with the truth of the children's dreams. The archive floods every colony channel. Emotional beat: love against duty, resolved in open rebellion.

chapters.title: Aftermath: Counting Forward
chapters.summary: Idris's POV. Hale, exposed by his own crew, stands down rather than fire on witnesses. The archive reaches millions; the children's shared dream becomes a shared inheritance. Amara is evacuated, alive but changed. Emotional beat: grief and relief indistinguishable.

chapters.title: Seeds in Open Ground
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. Back at the vault, Jude formally registers her name, her cargo, and the vault's location in the public ledger—ending seven years of invisibility by choice. The seeds will now be distributed, not hoarded. Emotional beat: vulnerability chosen freely.

chapters.title: The Dream Everyone Shares Now
chapters.summary: Nia's POV. Months later, the children still dream, but the dream has changed—it now shows the relay lit, the antenna whole, two figures walking its corridors. Nia understands they aren't receiving a signal anymore; they're keeping a memory warm. Emotional beat: memory as communal care.

chapters.title: Coral and the Horizon
chapters.summary: Jude and Amara's alternating POV, closing chapter. On the rebuilt relay's observation deck, they watch colony ships carry seedlings toward new worlds. Amara asks what Jude will do now; Jude answers: stop hauling cargo, start planting. The horizon is no longer something to flee. Emotional beat: arrival, at last.
